query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an α + β dual-phase alloy with low hardness and poor friction and wear properties under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Earlier studies explored redesigning the bulk alloy, which risks compromising its original advantages, and several surface-modification approaches. Traditional thermal spraying and thermal plating produced weak coatings with poor substrate bonding; composite coatings suffered from uneven constituent dispersion and weak interfaces; and laser cladding could generate intermetallic compounds, high residual stresses, cracks, and crazing. Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies reported improved hardness and wear resistance, but the broader requirements of compositional homogeneity, strong bonding, mechanical stability, and preservation of TC4’s beneficial properties remain. Formulate one neutral, testable hypothesis for an intervention that could satisfy these requirements. Specify the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding an optimized refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating incorporating controlled Ni content onto TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloy will improve surface hardness and reduce friction and wear under extreme, high-contact-stress conditions without compromising its intrinsic benefits.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) dual-phase alloy with inherently low hardness and poor friction/wear performance under extreme stresses.
generation.intervention: Apply a laser cladding process to deposit a refractory HEA coating—designed with a dominant BCC phase and controlled Ni addition—to the surface of TC4.
generation.conditions: High-contact stress and extreme service environments similar to aerospace or high-stress mechanical applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A multiphase coating structure featuring a refined grain size and a strong metallurgical bond with the TC4 substrate, where Ni is dissolved in the matrix to yield a solid solution and contribute to dispersion strengthening.
generation.mechanism: The HEA coating forms a densely bonded, refined microstructure with enhanced dispersion and solid solution strengthening due to Ni addition. This structural modification results in increased microhardness and a more stable interface that reduces abrasive and adhesive wear during high-stress operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with untreated TC4, the coated samples will exhibit significantly increased microhardness (potentially approaching or exceeding a twofold increase) and reduced friction coefficients and wear rates under simulated extreme service conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4 alloy that retains its usual low surface hardness and high wear rate under similar testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to manifest under operational regimes where high contact stresses and extreme environments are present; at significantly lower stresses or benign environments, the relative benefits of the coating may be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition (especially the precise Ni content) and the processing parameters (e.g., laser scanning speed and cladding thickness) require further optimization. Additionally, long-term thermal and mechanical stability in cyclic extreme environments has some uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of TC4 specimens: one set will be treated with laser cladding using the optimized refractory HEA coating (with controlled Ni content) and the other set will remain untreated. Subject both sets to standardized high-contact-stress friction and wear tests (e.g., reciprocating sliding tests) and perform microhardness measurements. Ensure that thermal cycling and environmental conditions simulate extreme service environments.
measurements: Surface microhardness using Vickers hardness testing
Wear volume or mass loss after a fixed number of cycles
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated TC4 samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement—defined as less than a 20% increase in microhardness and reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to untreated samples—then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Zhang et al. [] prepared a composite powder coating of TC4 and WC on the surface of TC4 titanium alloy. The results showed that adding 5%, 10%, and 15% WC content could help improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating, and the coating forming quality was good without cracks and other obvious defects. Chong et al. [] added 5% WC into AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy powder, and the research showed that WC enhanced the hardness of the AlCoCrFeNi coating, reduced the surface roughness, and improved the wear and corrosion resistance. Hu et al. used high-speed laser cladding to prepare a Ni/WC composite powder coating. The research showed that WC improves the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating and can refine the grain structure, and the decomposition of C and W elements precipitated from the coating played a solid solution strengthening role. Ma et al. [] studied the microstructure, microhardness, and wear resistance of a 60% WC-reinforced FeCoNiCr composite coating prepared by laser cladding. The results showed that the composite coating had good forming quality and better microhardness and wear resistance.

In this study, the surface of (Ti-6Al-4V)TC4 alloy was modified via laser cladding. The elemental composition of the coating was (TiAl)95−xCu5Nix, with Ni as the variable (where x = 0, 3, 6, and 9 at.%). Multi-principal alloy coatings were successfully prepared, and their constituent phases, microstructures, and chemical compositions were thoroughly investigated. The hardness and wear resistance of the coatings were analyzed, and the compositions and interfacial characteristics of the different phases were examined via transmission electron microscopy. The analysis revealed that Ni formed a solid solution and a eutectic structure in the Ti(Al, Cu)2 phase. These findings provide valuable insights into the coating properties. Moreover, reciprocal dry sliding friction experiments were conducted to investigate the wear mechanism. The results revealed a significant increase in wear resistance owing to the formation of a Ni solid solution and changes in the coating structure. Additionally, tensile tests demonstrated that the tensile strength of the coatings initially increased and then decreased with varying Ni content. Multi-principal element alloy coatings were created on the TC4 surface using laser cladding techniques. The addition of Cu and Ni to TiAl alloy powders improved the wear resistance and tensile properties of the coatings. The following conclusions were reached:The coating mainly consists of Ti3Al and Ti(Al, Cu)2 phases, with Ni fully dissolved in the Ti(Al, Cu)2 phase and some TiAl phases, resulting in a multiphase structure that effectively balances strength and toughness. A strong interface is observed between the Ti3Al and Ti(Al, Cu)2 phases. At a microscopic level, the incorporation of Ni alters the phase composition of the coating. Ni, a solid solution within the Ti(Al, Cu)2 phase, induces a solid solution hardening effect, which improves the various properties of the coating.Adding Ni to TiAlCu improves the various properties of the coatings through solid solution strengthening. With increasing Ni content, the hardness increases, while wear resistance and mechanical properties initially improve and then decline.
